CAN FD interface board

Altium Designer · IGVC team · September 2025 – March 2026

A 2-layer board that connects a microcontroller to a CAN bus over SPI, so the vehicle’s subsystems can talk to each other.

What I did

  • Completed the full design cycle: schematic capture, component selection, and PCB layout in Altium Designer.
  • Used the MCP2518FD controller, ATA6561 transceiver, and AP7583Q LDO for onboard power.
  • Replaced discontinued parts from an open-source reference design.

How I verified it

  • Validated the crystal oscillator circuit on breakout and perfboard prototypes before fabrication.
  • Confirmed two-node Pico 2 communication at 250 kbit/s, reading the bus with an oscilloscope CAN decoder; the firmware also runs at 500 kbit/s.

Redox flow battery data acquisition

University of Burgos, Spain · Undergraduate research · June – July 2026

The goal was a clean, logged record of a redox flow battery’s open-circuit voltage, to build a dataset for state-of-charge estimation. The signal is only hundreds of millivolts, so noise from the measurement setup itself matters. I measured it differentially with a 16-bit ADS1115 ADC and went through three hardware architectures to get clean data.

Phase I: Arduino and ADS1115

The ADC needs a ground shared with the Arduino, or its differential reading relative to its own ground is undefined. That same connection carried the Arduino’s switching and USB power noise straight into the battery signal, a ground loop. I ruled out filtering, because at this signal size it risks removing real signal along with the noise. Instead I placed a Pololu ISO1640 digital isolator between the Arduino and the ADC and powered the ADC from an isolated 5 V supply, which broke the shared ground path and gave accurate differential readings.

Phase II: Raspberry Pi PLC

I replaced the Arduino with an Industrial Shields Raspberry Pi PLC (a Raspberry Pi 4 in an industrial enclosure), powered from 24 V DC, with a Traco module stepping down to 5.1 V for the ADC. A Pololu ISO02A isolator separated the ADC from the PLC’s ground. Moving to Python simplified the voltage calculation and data logging. The ground-loop and ground-detection problems were resolved, but voltage fluctuations specific to the PLC platform remained even with isolation in place. Because they appeared only after PLC integration, electromagnetic interference from the PLC is the likely cause; I have not yet confirmed it.

Phase III: hybrid

To keep Phase I’s clean acquisition and Phase II’s Python logging, the Arduino and ADS1115 from Phase I now acquire the data and send it to the PLC over USB serial for storage and analysis. I compared the noise of the Arduino and potentiostat measurements using a rolling standard deviation and a frequency spectrum over about 35,000 seconds of data. Both show a near-zero baseline apart from a few isolated spikes.

Skills used

  • Differential ADC measurement, grounding, galvanic and digital isolation.
  • Python data logging on a Raspberry Pi PLC, Arduino firmware, serial communication.
  • Noise analysis in MATLAB: rolling standard deviation and frequency spectrum.

Two-phase interleaved buck converterIn progress

LTspice · Power Electronics course · January 2026 – present

A CPU/GPU voltage regulator design that converts 12 V to 1.1 V across two interleaved phases. The schematic below is my current working version, and I am revising the design.

What I did

  • Built two synchronous buck phases with 3.3 µH inductors and a shared 470 µF output capacitor.
  • Drive each phase from its own 100 kHz sawtooth ramp, offset by half a period for 180° interleaving.
  • Built voltage-mode control: an error amplifier compares the output to a 1.1 V reference, and LTC6752 comparators turn its output into the PWM duty cycle.
  • Redesigning the compensator using AC loop-gain analysis to meet phase-margin and load-transient targets.

Hardwired e-stopIn design

IGVC autonomous vehicle · September 2026 – present

A safety circuit that stops the vehicle without depending on software. I am designing it now; it is not built or tested yet.

Design approach

  • A normally-closed, dual-channel emergency button, so a broken wire or a failed channel stops the vehicle.
  • A main power relay that de-energizes the vehicle, plus a separate power break on the motor controller.
  • No software in the stop path.

Team role

I lead a 5-person hardware subteam building the vehicle’s electrical subsystems: motor controller, battery management system with overvoltage protection, e-stop, and sensors. I set weekly goals, assign tasks, and manage the schedule while we convert a stripped scooter frame into the vehicle platform. I tested the vehicle motor with an existing H-bridge motor controller board.
